'''Deborah Beth Zamble''' (October 5, 1971 – July 6, 2020) was a Canadian chemist and Canada Research Chair in Biological Chemistry at the [[University of Toronto]]. Her research considered how bacteria processed metal nutrients.

== Early life and education ==
Zamble was born in [[Kingston, Ontario]]. She attended the [[University of Toronto]] for her undergraduate studies, where she worked in the lab of the [[Bibudhendra Sarkar]]. Zamble was a graduate student at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], where she worked with [[Stephen J. Lippard]] on [[cisplatin]], an anti-cancer drug. Her research considered the role of [[p53]] in the cellular response to the drug. Zamble was a postdoctoral fellow at the [[Harvard Medical School]], where she worked alongside [[Christopher T. Walsh]]. At the Harvard Medical School, Zamble worked on the microcin B17 synthetase.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zamble|first1=Deborah B.|last2=McClure|first2=Craig P.|last3=Penner-Hahn|first3=James E.|last4=Walsh|first4=Christopher T.|date=2000-12-01|title=The McbB Component of Microcin B17 Synthetase Is a Zinc Metalloprotein|journal=Biochemistry|volume=39|issue=51|pages=16190–16199|doi=10.1021/bi001398e|pmid=11123948|issn=0006-2960}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Zamble returned to [[Canada]] in 2001, where she was made a Canada Research Chair in Biological Chemistry.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Canada's new government invests in research and projects to improve quality of life for Canadians {{!}} Innovation.ca|url=https://www.innovation.ca/about/press-release/canadas-new-government-invests-research-and-projects-improve-quality-life|access-date=2020-07-08|website=www.innovation.ca|archive-date=2020-07-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200708200436/https://www.innovation.ca/about/press-release/canadas-new-government-invests-research-and-projects-improve-quality-life|url-status=dead}}</ref> Here she investigated how bacteria process metal nutrients, with a focus on the uptake of nickel.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Deborah B. Zamble|url=http://biochemistry.utoronto.ca/person/deborah-b-zamble/|access-date=2020-07-08|website=Biochemistry, University of Toronto|archive-date=2020-07-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200708201042/http://biochemistry.utoronto.ca/person/deborah-b-zamble/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Transition metals are essential to the structure and function of biological systems, but can be toxic if they are allowed to accumulate. To mitigate this, cells make use of metalloproteins to regulate the use of each metal. In particular, Zamble studies the bacteria ''[[Escherichia coli]]'' and ''[[Helicobacter pylori]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Research {{!}} Zamble Lab|url=https://sites.chem.utoronto.ca/zamblelab/content/research|access-date=2020-07-08|website=sites.chem.utoronto.ca}}</ref>

== Academic service ==
Zamble served on the executive board of the [[Royal Canadian Institute]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Executive & Board|url=https://www.rciscience.ca/executive-board|access-date=2020-07-08|website=Royal Canadian Institute for Science|language=en-US|archive-date=2021-10-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028185908/https://www.rciscience.ca/executive-board|url-status=dead}}</ref> She served on the editorial boards of the [[Journal of Biological Chemistry]]<ref>{{Cite web|title=Journal of Biological Inorganic Chemistry|url=https://www.springer.com/journal/775/editors|access-date=2020-07-08|website=Springer|language=en}}</ref> and [[Metallomics (journal)|Metallomics]].<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2014-12-24|title=Metallomics Editorial Board profiles|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2015/mt/c4mt90048k|journal=Metallomics|language=en|volume=7|issue=1|pages=12–14|doi=10.1039/C4MT90048K|issn=1756-591X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Zamble was involved with recreating the biological chemistry curriculum at the [[University of Toronto]], leading a second year course that incorporated her enthusiasm for cooking.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=News {{!}} Department of Chemistry|url=https://www.chemistry.utoronto.ca/news/remembering-deborah-zamble|access-date=2020-07-08|website=www.chemistry.utoronto.ca|date=7 July 2020}}</ref>

On July 6, 2020, Zamble died of an unexpected [[brain haemorrhage]].<ref name=":1" />
